query: Using molecular dynamics simulations of a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix, investigate the thermomechanical response during nanoindentation (30 Å depth, 10 m/s velocity) at 300 K, 600 K, 900 K, and 1200 K. Existing data suggests that while dislocation density decreases at 600 K (increasing elastic modulus), rapid lattice disorder emerges at higher temperatures, correlating with a sharp drop in hardness and wear resistance. Hypothesize the specific sequence of microstructural events (e.g., stacking fault annihilation, dislocation starvation, amorphization onset) that causes the friction coefficient to spike and the material to lose wear resistance above 900 K. Propose a falsification experiment using hexagonal close-packed (HCP) atom counting and dislocation line length analysis to distinguish between thermal softening due to disorder versus mechanical annealing effects.

generation.target_system: Single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy (FCC solid solution) coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix, subjected to nanoindentation (30 Å depth, 10 m/s velocity) at 300 K, 600 K, 900 K, and 1200 K.

evidence_appraisal.difference_from_target: Different alloy composition (Mn vs Cu), different geometry (nanowire vs coating), different loading mode (tensile/superplasticity vs nanoindentation), but same FCC HEA class and temperature-dependent deformation mechanisms (twinning, phase transformation).
evidence_appraisal.reason: The mechanism of deformation twinning and FCC-HCP transformation is relevant to the target FCC HEA, but the specific geometry and loading rate differ. The temperature trend of maintaining strength at high T is relevant.

evidence_appraisal.difference_from_target: Different alloy composition (Mn vs Cu), but same FCC HEA class. Focuses on stacking fault energy (SFE) and magnetic effects on phase stability (FCC vs HCP) as a function of temperature.
evidence_appraisal.reason: Directly addresses the temperature dependence of stacking fault energy and the FCC-HCP phase transition in FCC HEAs, which is the core mechanism for the hypothesized disorder and softening in the target system.

evidence_appraisal.reason: The observed transition in deformation mechanisms from twinning to dynamic recovery/recrystallization at high temperatures (700°C+) provides a direct analog for the loss of hardness and wear resistance above 900 K in the target single-crystal system.

generation.hypothesis: The spike in friction coefficient and loss of wear resistance above 900 K in the FeNiCrCoCu single-crystal coating is caused by a sequential cascade of thermally activated microstructural events: (1) At ~600-900 K, the stacking fault energy (SFE) increases significantly, suppressing the formation of partial dislocations and deformation twins, leading to a temporary increase in elastic modulus and dislocation starvation (consistent with PMC6093928 and PMC8398136). (2) Above 900 K, the thermal energy overcomes the lattice distortion barrier, triggering rapid lattice disorder and a local FCC-to-HCP phase transformation (or amorphization onset) driven by the negative or near-zero SFE at these specific local strain states, as predicted by the temperature-dependent SFE trends in PMC6093928. (3) This disorder facilitates the nucleation of HCP nuclei and the annihilation of stacking faults, effectively acting as a mechanical annealing process that eliminates the dislocation network required for work hardening. (4) The resulting amorphous or highly disordered HCP-rich surface layer exhibits low shear strength and high adhesion to the indenter, causing the friction coefficient to spike. (5) The loss of structural integrity (amorphization) leads to a sharp drop in hardness and wear resistance as the material can no longer sustain the contact load, transitioning from elastic/plastic deformation to flow-like behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix, FCC solid solution, defect-free or low dislocation density prior to indentation.
generation.intervention: Nanoindentation at a depth of 30 Å and velocity of 10 m/s, performed at temperatures of 300 K, 600 K, 900 K, and 1200 K.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 300 K to 1200 K; Indentation depth: 30 Å; Indentation velocity: 10 m/s; Environment: Vacuum or inert gas (implied for MD simulation).
generation.structural_mediator: Stacking fault energy (SFE) evolution, FCC-HCP phase transformation, dislocation annihilation, and amorphization onset.
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials science principles and supported by PMC6093928 (SFE temperature dependence) and PMC7229066 (high-T mechanism transition). The mechanism involves the temperature-dependent increase in SFE suppressing twinning at intermediate temperatures, followed by thermal activation of lattice disorder and FCC-to-HCP transformation at >900 K. This transformation, coupled with the high entropy of mixing, leads to a loss of long-range order (amorphization) and dislocation starvation, reducing the material's ability to harden and increasing adhesion/friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: At 300 K and 600 K: High hardness, low friction, deformation dominated by partial dislocations and twinning. At 900 K: Onset of friction spike, hardness drop, emergence of HCP phase and amorphous regions. At 1200 K: Maximum friction coefficient, minimum hardness, extensive amorphization/HCP transformation, and catastrophic wear failure due to loss of structural cohesion.
generation.baseline: Standard FCC HEA behavior where hardness typically decreases monotonically with temperature due to thermal activation of dislocation glide, but without the specific spike in friction caused by phase transformation and amorphization.
generation.boundary: Valid for single-crystal FCC HEAs with high configurational entropy and moderate atomic size mismatch. May not apply to BCC HEAs or multiphase alloys where precipitation hardening dominates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold for the FCC-to-HCP transition and amorphization onset in FeNiCrCoCu may vary due to the specific Cu content and the high strain rate of nanoindentation. The magnitude of the friction spike is uncertain without direct measurement of the interfacial shear strength of the amorphous layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform molecular dynamics simulations of the FeNiCrCoCu single crystal under identical nanoindentation conditions (30 Å, 10 m/s) at 900 K and 1200 K, but with a modified interatomic potential that artificially suppresses the FCC-to-HCP phase transformation (e.g., by increasing the stacking fault energy artificially).
measurements: Count of HCP atoms (using common neighbor analysis or CNA)
Radial distribution function (RDF) to detect amorphization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hypothesis is correct, suppressing the FCC-to-HCP transformation should prevent the spike in the friction coefficient and the sharp drop in hardness at 900 K and 1200 K. Specifically, the HCP atom count should remain near zero, and the COF should remain low (similar to 600 K levels) despite the high temperature. If the COF still spikes and hardness drops despite the suppression of HCP formation, the mechanism is likely dominated by pure thermal softening or amorphization unrelated to the HCP phase.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
